ground_truth_methodology: Established by directly reading the cloned source at the pinned commit (Read/Grep on benchmarks/real_world_python/repos/flask), using general knowledge of the Flask codebase as a starting hypothesis only where it pointed at the right file, then verified line-for-line against the actual clone. Veyra was NOT used to produce any of this file.

queries.query: Where is the Flask application class defined?
queries.ground_truth_location: src/flask/app.py:110 (class Flask(App)); base class App at src/flask/sansio/app.py:59
queries.expected_answer_summary: flask.app.Flask, defined at app.py:110, subclasses flask.sansio.app.App (sansio/app.py:59).

queries.query: Which class implements Flask's default (cookie-based) session storage?
queries.expected_answer_summary: SecureCookieSessionInterface (sessions.py:284) is the default session_interface assigned on the Flask class (app.py:253); it produces SecureCookieSession (sessions.py:57) instances.

queries.query: Where is the Request class that Flask uses for incoming HTTP requests defined?
queries.expected_answer_summary: flask.wrappers.Request, defined at wrappers.py:18, subclassing werkzeug's RequestBase.

queries.query: What does the @app.route decorator actually call to register a URL rule?
queries.ground_truth_location: Scaffold.route at sansio/scaffold.py:344 calls self.add_url_rule(...); the real implementation used at runtime is App.add_url_rule at sansio/app.py:605 (Scaffold.add_url_rule at scaffold.py:376 exists but App overrides it)
queries.expected_answer_summary: route() (Scaffold, scaffold.py:344) is a decorator factory that calls self.add_url_rule(rule, endpoint, f, **options); on a Flask app the method resolution order means App.add_url_rule (sansio/app.py:605) is what actually runs, and it registers a werkzeug Rule on self.url_map.
queries.notes: multi-hop: requires following route() to add_url_rule() and then recognizing which of the two add_url_rule definitions (Scaffold vs App) actually executes via inheritance/override.

queries.query: What class does Flask's Blueprint inherit from?
queries.ground_truth_location: src/flask/blueprints.py:18 -- class Blueprint(SansioBlueprint), where SansioBlueprint is flask.sansio.blueprints.Blueprint imported under an alias (blueprints.py:10); that class itself is defined at sansio/blueprints.py:119 as class Blueprint(Scaffold).
queries.expected_answer_summary: flask.blueprints.Blueprint subclasses flask.sansio.blueprints.Blueprint (imported as SansioBlueprint), which itself subclasses Scaffold.
queries.notes: tricky because two different classes are both literally named Blueprint in different modules, connected via an import alias -- tests whether retrieval distinguishes them.

queries.query: How does Flask dispatch an incoming WSGI request to the correct view function, end to end?
queries.ground_truth_location: app.py:1569 wsgi_app -> app.py:995 full_dispatch_request -> app.py:1369 preprocess_request -> app.py:969 dispatch_request (matches the URL via the request context's url_adapter) -> app.py:1024 finalize_request -> app.py:1397 process_response
queries.expected_answer_summary: wsgi_app() is the WSGI entry point; it pushes a request context and calls full_dispatch_request(), which runs preprocess_request(), then dispatch_request() (which resolves the matched URL rule's endpoint and calls the view function), then finalize_request() which calls process_response().
queries.notes: multi-hop architecture question spanning 5 methods in one file; a shallow retrieval that surfaces only one of these methods should not be scored as fully correct.

queries.query: How does Flask sign and verify session cookies to prevent tampering?
queries.ground_truth_location: src/flask/sessions.py -- SecureCookieSessionInterface (class at 284) uses get_signing_serializer to build an itsdangerous serializer keyed on app.secret_key; Flask delegates the actual cryptographic signing to the third-party itsdangerous library, it does not implement HMAC/signing itself.
queries.expected_answer_summary: SecureCookieSessionInterface builds an itsdangerous URLSafeTimedSerializer from app.secret_key via get_signing_serializer(); Flask itself only wires this up -- the actual signing/verification algorithm lives in the itsdangerous dependency, not in the Flask repository.
queries.notes: partially a negative/boundary case: the low-level signing algorithm itself is NOT in this repository (it's in itsdangerous). A correct answer should say so rather than claiming Flask implements the cryptography itself.

queries.query: What happens when app.run() is called with debug=True?
queries.expected_answer_summary: Flask.run() (app.py:633) sets debug on app.config if passed, then delegates to werkzeug.serving.run_simple with use_debugger/use_reloader enabled when debug is true, which enables the interactive debugger and the auto-reloader.

queries.query: What does Flask do when a request comes in for a URL that doesn't match any registered rule?
queries.ground_truth_location: src/flask/sansio/app.py:563 (raise_routing_exception); the underlying NotFound comes from werkzeug's MapAdapter.match() raising werkzeug.routing.exceptions.NotFound, caught and handled by Flask's exception-handling machinery in app.py.
queries.expected_answer_summary: The werkzeug URL adapter's match() raises a routing exception (typically NotFound); Flask's raise_routing_exception (sansio/app.py:563) re-raises it so the app's normal error-handling / 404 response path takes over.

queries.query: If a Flask view function raises an unhandled exception, where should I look to see how Flask decides what response to send back?
queries.expected_answer_summary: full_dispatch_request() catches exceptions from dispatch_request() and routes them to handle_user_exception() (app.py:868), which looks for a registered errorhandler; if nothing handles it (or it's not an HTTPException) it falls through to handle_exception() (app.py:900), which builds the generic 500 response.

queries.query: Where would I investigate if Flask's test_client() isn't preserving cookies across multiple requests in a test?
queries.ground_truth_location: src/flask/testing.py:109 (class FlaskClient(Client)) -- cookie persistence across requests is a werkzeug.test.Client feature FlaskClient inherits; src/flask/testing.py:27 (EnvironBuilder) builds the per-request WSGI environ.
queries.expected_answer_summary: FlaskClient (testing.py:109) is Flask's test client; cookie-jar behavior across requests comes from the werkzeug.test.Client base class it extends, with EnvironBuilder (testing.py:27) constructing each request's environ.

queries.query: How does registering a Blueprint on a Flask app connect the blueprint's routes to the app's URL map?
queries.ground_truth_location: App.register_blueprint (sansio/app.py:570) calls blueprint.register(self, options); Blueprint.register (sansio/blueprints.py:273) builds a BlueprintSetupState and calls each deferred function recorded via blueprint.record()/route() registrations, ultimately invoking BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule (sansio/blueprints.py:87), which calls the app's own add_url_rule with the blueprint's url_prefix applied.
queries.expected_answer_summary: App.register_blueprint() (sansio/app.py:570) calls Blueprint.register() (sansio/blueprints.py:273), which replays the blueprint's deferred route registrations against a BlueprintSetupState; BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule() (sansio/blueprints.py:87) prefixes the blueprint's rules and calls back into the app's own add_url_rule, which is what actually adds them to app.url_map.
queries.notes: genuinely cross-file: the answer requires combining app.py's register_blueprint with two different pieces of sansio/blueprints.py.

queries.query: Where does Flask implement CSRF protection for form submissions?
queries.expected_answer_summary: Flask itself does not implement CSRF protection anywhere in this repository. That functionality is provided by the separate Flask-WTF extension, which is not part of this codebase.
queries.notes: negative/boundary query -- correct behavior is to report that no such implementation exists in this repository, not to invent one or point at an unrelated security-adjacent module (e.g. sessions.py) as if it were CSRF protection.

queries.query: Where is Flask's built-in ORM or database layer implemented?
queries.expected_answer_summary: Flask has no built-in ORM or database layer in this repository. That is provided by separate extensions (e.g. Flask-SQLAlchemy), not by Flask core.
